plan: Complete enhanced-ACT literary narrative (CLD-P-ACT-R-000040, 'Heavyweight'), an original story about two elderly neighbors who rival each other at a county-fair pumpkin weigh-off; one protects the other's pumpkin in a storm. Checked against every ACT Reading passage title and opening: not a mentor/apprentice, bakery, inventory, translator, or parent-child storyline. 10 questions. Relabelled to the blind solvers' rating where it was lower: R040-01 medium→easy, R040-02 hard→medium, R040-04 medium→easy, R040-05 medium→easy, R040-06 hard→medium, R040-07 medium→easy, R040-08 hard→medium, R040-10 medium→easy.

passages.title: Heavyweight
passages.text:
For eleven Septembers, the heaviest pumpkin at the Corley County Fair had come from one of two backyards on Mill Road, and the two backyards shared a fence. Ruth Okafor had won six of those years and Dale Pruitt five, and neither of them could tell you the other's numbers without also telling you, unprompted, what had gone wrong for the other that year: the hailstorm, the split stem, the summer Dale's hose timer failed while he was at his daughter's wedding.

Ruth was seventy-three and did not consider herself competitive. She considered herself thorough. She kept a notebook for each plant—soil temperature at dawn, inches of growth, gallons of water—and in the evenings she sat on her back step with the notebook open and pretended not to listen to Dale talking to his pumpkin on the other side of the fence. He talked to it the way some people talk to horses, low and steady, and he swore it made a difference. Ruth had told her sister on the phone that this was unscientific, which was true, and that it was ridiculous, which she was less sure of.

This year both plants had done well. Ruth's was the largest she had ever grown, and from the way Dale had started whispering to his, she guessed his was too.

The storm came the night before the weigh-off. Ruth woke at two to rain hitting the windows sideways and went out in her slicker with a flashlight to check the tarps over her own plant. They were holding. Then she swung the light toward the fence and saw that the plastic sheeting over Dale's hoop house had torn loose and was snapping in the wind like a sail, and that water was pooling around the base of his pumpkin. His windows were dark. His truck was gone; she remembered then that he had driven to the city to pick up his grandson.

She stood there long enough for the rain to find its way down the back of her collar. A pumpkin left sitting in water overnight could soften on the bottom, and a soft spot could get it disqualified. She thought of the notebooks, of the six ribbons in the hall closet, and of the satisfaction—she would not pretend it wasn't there—of the one year she had beaten him by more than a hundred pounds. Then she went to the garage for the stepladder and a box of clamps.

It took her forty minutes. She dug a shallow trench with a trowel to lead the water away, and she clamped the sheeting back onto the frame, and when she finished she was soaked through and her hands were shaking, only partly from the cold. She did not leave a note.

At the weigh-off the next afternoon, Dale's pumpkin came in three pounds heavier than hers. The crowd cheered, someone handed Dale the ribbon, and Ruth clapped with everyone else and found, to her surprise, that she meant it, or at least most of it.

That evening she was on her back step with the notebook when she heard him on the other side of the fence. He was not talking to a pumpkin. "Somebody dug a trench in my hoop house last night," he said. "Clamped the plastic down, too. Nice work. Not the way I'd have done the clamps."

"I'm sure I wouldn't know," Ruth said.

There was a long pause. "Next year," Dale said, "I'm going to beat you by a hundred."

Ruth turned to a clean page and wrote the date at the top. "You can try," she said.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best describes the passage as a whole?

choices.A: A gardener's long friendship with her neighbor ends after a dispute over a county fair contest.
choices.B: A gardener quietly protects her longtime rival's entry before a contest, and the rivalry continues afterward.
choices.C: Two gardeners compare their methods for growing pumpkins and agree that talking to plants makes little difference.
choices.D: A storm destroys one gardener's pumpkin, and her neighbor wins the county fair contest for the first time.

candidates.evidence: She did not leave a note.
candidates.explanation: The passage builds to Ruth's decision to save Dale's pumpkin in the storm, then shows Dale winning, recognizing her help indirectly, and challenging her for next year.

A.rationale: The neighbors remain on speaking terms, and nothing ends; Dale even promises to compete again next year.

C.rationale: Their methods are mentioned briefly, and they never discuss or agree on whether talking to plants helps.

D.rationale: Ruth's tarps held, and Dale had already won five times before.

hints: What is the central event, and what happens after it?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the beginning, middle, and end in one sentence.

candidates.remember: A whole-passage answer must fit the central event and the ending.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 2, the statement that Ruth "did not consider herself competitive. She considered herself thorough" mainly suggests that Ruth:

choices.A: is not interested in the contest and grows pumpkins only for her own records.
choices.B: believes her neighbor's methods are more thorough than her own.
choices.C: has recently decided to stop competing against her neighbor.
choices.D: describes her careful habits in a way that downplays how much winning matters to her.

candidates.evidence: of the satisfaction—she would not pretend it wasn't there—of the one year she had beaten him
candidates.explanation: The paired sentences present Ruth's own view of herself, and the rest of the passage (the remembered satisfaction of beating Dale by a hundred pounds, the six ribbons) shows that winning matters more to her than "thorough" admits.

A.rationale: Paragraph 5 shows she cares about her ribbons and enjoyed beating Dale, so she is interested in winning.

B.rationale: She calls Dale's habit "unscientific"; nothing suggests she thinks he is more thorough.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests she plans to stop; the ending shows her preparing for next year.

hints: Does the rest of the passage support Ruth's view of herself?

strategy.explanation: Compare what Ruth says about herself with what she does and feels later.

candidates.remember: When a narrator reports a character's self-image, check it against the character's actions.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Dale's windows were dark on the night of the storm because he:

choices.A: had driven to the city to pick up his grandson.
choices.B: was asleep and did not hear the rain.
choices.D: had gone to the fairgrounds to prepare for the weigh-off.

candidates.evidence: she remembered then that he had driven to the city to pick up his grandson
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 states that his truck was gone because he had driven to the city to pick up his grandson.

B.rationale: The passage says his truck was gone and he had driven to the city.

C.rationale: The wedding was in an earlier summer, when his hose timer failed.

D.rationale: The passage says he went to pick up his grandson, not to the fair.

hints: Find the sentence right after "His windows were dark."
candidates.remember: Detail questions are answered by a specific sentence; watch for details from other years.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 4, the description of the plastic sheeting "snapping in the wind like a sail" mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that Dale had designed his hoop house to resemble a boat.
choices.B: indicate that the storm was ending and the wind was growing calmer.
choices.C: show how violently the loose sheeting was being whipped around by the storm.
choices.D: explain why Ruth's own tarps had been torn loose by the wind.

candidates.evidence: had torn loose and was snapping in the wind like a sail
candidates.explanation: A sail snaps loudly and hard in strong wind, so the comparison conveys how forcefully the torn sheeting was flapping, which is why the pumpkin was exposed to the rain.

A.rationale: The comparison describes the sheeting's motion in the wind, not the hoop house's design.

B.rationale: Rain is still hitting the windows sideways; nothing suggests the storm is ending.

D.rationale: Ruth's tarps "were holding"; only Dale's sheeting tore loose.

hints: What does a sail do in a strong wind?

strategy.explanation: Picture the comparison, then match its effect.

candidates.remember: A simile usually sharpens a picture of what is happening.

candidates.stem: The first paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: establish a long, closely matched rivalry in which each gardener keeps track of the other's setbacks.
choices.B: explain the rules that the county fair uses to weigh and judge the pumpkins entered in its contest.
choices.C: introduce the storm that later threatens both gardeners' pumpkins on the night before the weigh-off.
choices.D: suggest that Dale has usually been the more careful and successful of the two gardeners.

candidates.evidence: Ruth Okafor had won six of those years and Dale Pruitt five
candidates.explanation: The paragraph gives the near-even record (six wins to five) and shows that each can recite the other's bad luck, establishing a close, long-running rivalry.

B.rationale: No contest rules appear in the paragraph.

C.rationale: The storm is not mentioned until paragraph 4.

D.rationale: Ruth has won six times to Dale's five.

hints: What does the record of wins show?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the rest of the story needs from this opening.

candidates.remember: Opening paragraphs usually set up the situation the story develops.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 2, the narrator's comment that Ruth was "less sure" Dale's habit was ridiculous most strongly suggests that Ruth:

choices.A: has started talking to her own pumpkin in secret when Dale is away.
choices.B: believes that talking to plants is scientifically proven to work.
choices.C: wants her sister to stop asking her so many questions about her neighbor.
choices.D: privately suspects there may be more to Dale's habit than she admits.

candidates.evidence: and pretended not to listen to Dale talking to his pumpkin
candidates.explanation: Ruth accepts that the habit is unscientific but doubts it is ridiculous, and she "pretended not to listen" to it, which suggests a fondness she does not admit.

A.rationale: Nothing says she talks to her plant; she keeps a notebook.

B.rationale: She calls the habit "unscientific," which the narrator says is true.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests she wants her sister to stop asking.

hints: Why would she pretend not to listen?

strategy.explanation: Combine her doubt with how she listens.

candidates.remember: A character's hesitation often reveals feelings she will not state.

candidates.stem: The statement that Ruth "meant it, or at least most of it" when she clapped (paragraph 7) suggests that Ruth:

choices.A: regretted having helped Dale protect his pumpkin the night before.
choices.B: was mostly glad for Dale but still felt some disappointment at losing.
choices.C: was pretending to be happy while feeling only anger.
choices.D: did not realize at first that Dale's pumpkin had beaten hers.

candidates.evidence: found, to her surprise, that she meant it, or at least most of it
candidates.explanation: "Meant it" shows real gladness; "at least most of it" admits a small leftover disappointment.

A.rationale: "Most of it" means her applause was largely sincere, not that she regretted helping.

C.rationale: She meant "most of it," so her happiness was largely genuine.

D.rationale: She clapped for Dale's win, so she knew the result.

hints: What does "most of it" leave out?

strategy.explanation: Predict both parts of her feeling before reading choices.

candidates.stem: Taken together, Dale's remarks in paragraphs 8 and 10 most strongly suggest that he:

choices.A: believes a stranger repaired his hoop house and wants Ruth to help find that person.
choices.B: is angry that someone touched his hoop house without asking.
choices.C: knows Ruth protected his pumpkin and shows his thanks by treating her as a rival again.
choices.D: plans to stop competing because he thinks he won unfairly.

candidates.evidence: Not the way I'd have done the clamps
candidates.explanation: Dale addresses the repair to Ruth, praises and teases it, then issues a challenge that echoes her old hundred-pound win; his thanks takes the form of keeping the rivalry going.

A.rationale: He speaks across the fence to Ruth and teases her about the clamps, which suggests he knows she did it.

B.rationale: He calls it "Nice work," so he is not angry.

D.rationale: He promises to beat her by a hundred next year.

hints: Who is Dale talking to, and why mention the clamps?
candidates.remember: Characters often express gratitude indirectly; look at whom they speak to and how.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 1, the word "unprompted" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: without also telling you, unprompted, what had gone wrong for the other that year
candidates.explanation: Each gardener volunteers the other's bad luck even when no one asks, showing how closely they watch each other.

A.rationale: Nothing in the sentence concerns payment.

C.rationale: Each can recite the other's setbacks in detail, so uncertainty does not fit.

D.rationale: The word describes when they offer the information, not their tone.

hints: Did anyone ask them about the other's setbacks?

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with your own phrase first.

candidates.remember: A prompt is a cue to speak; "unprompted" means with no cue.

candidates.stem: The final paragraph suggests that Ruth:

choices.A: has decided to stop keeping records of her plants.
choices.B: believes Dale cannot possibly beat her by a hundred pounds.
choices.C: plans to tell Dale that she was the one who fixed his hoop house.
choices.D: accepts Dale's challenge and is already preparing for next year's contest.

candidates.evidence: Ruth turned to a clean page and wrote the date at the top.
candidates.explanation: Starting a fresh page in her growing notebook and answering "You can try" shows that Ruth accepts the challenge and is beginning her records for the next season.

A.rationale: She writes the date on a clean page, so she is continuing her records.

B.rationale: "You can try" is a challenge, not a claim that it is impossible.

C.rationale: She has just declined to take credit, and nothing suggests she will.

hints: What is the notebook used for?

strategy.explanation: Recall what the notebook is from paragraph 2.

candidates.remember: Small actions at an ending often carry the story's meaning.

revision_log.reason: Round-1 blind solves matched every key; both noted overlaps: R040-08 and R040-09 tested the same point (Ruth helped without admitting it, Dale knows), and R040-04's key ('how much beating Dale pleased her') gave away R040-02. Replaced 04 with a simile-function item and 09 with a vocabulary item ('unprompted'); added a paragraph reference to 06's stem and tightened its key. Passage unchanged. Whole batch re-solved blind.
